summary: Children aged 9-10 learn to draw and identify points, lines, line segments, rays, angles (right/acute/obtuse) and parallel/perpendicular lines, and to find these inside two-dimensional figures (CCSS 4.G.A.1). The core teaching work is separating each defining property from its incidental appearance: an angle is the amount of opening at the vertex regardless of how long the arms are drawn; parallel means lines stay the same distance apart and never meet, and segments or sides are parallel when they lie on such lines, whatever their drawn lengths; perpendicular means a square corner at any orientation. Two deep visual habits must be dislodged — judging angle size by arm length or endpoint gap, and recognising right angles/perpendicularity only when lines sit 'upright'. Vocabulary is taught through drawing and marking, not memorised definitions.
misconceptions: Angle size depends on arm length or the distance between the arms' endpoints — a wider-drawn angle with longer rays is judged 'bigger' (arm-length / whole-object bias)
'Angle is the distance between the ends of the lines' — treating the gap between endpoints as the measure
Parallel lines must be the same length, so a trapezoid's unequal parallel sides are rejected as not parallel
Right angles and perpendicular lines are only recognised in horizontal-vertical (upright) orientation and missed when the figure is tilted
A ray and a line segment are the same, or a 'line' stops at the drawn endpoints rather than extending

activities.title: Stretch the arm, keep the angle
steps: Swing one ray of a fixed-vertex angle open to roughly 130° and name it obtuse.

Grab the end of that arm as drawn (the ray itself goes on forever; only its drawn part changes) and drag it outward along the same direction so the drawn arm gets much longer, while watching the degree readout stay at 130°.
State what changed (arm length) and what did not change (the opening at the vertex), concluding the angle size is unchanged.
Overlay two angles vertex-on-vertex with arms coinciding, then extend or shorten one arm to confirm the opening is the same.
activities.insight: An angle is the amount of opening (or turn) at the vertex, not the length of its arms or the distance between their endpoints.

activities.title: Parallel at any length, perpendicular at any tilt
steps: Draw (or drag) two line segments that stay the same distance apart (so they would never meet however far they were extended), deliberately making one shorter than the other, and label them parallel.
Draw rail or road-line segments of clearly different lengths but constant separation, and explain why they are still parallel (extended, they would never meet).

Draw two lines meeting at a square corner and label them perpendicular; verify the corner by fitting the corner of a card or a set-square into it, and repeat with perpendicular pairs drawn at several different tilts.
Rotate the whole figure so a right-angled corner tips off-axis, and confirm with the card corner that it is still a right angle; rotate back to check.
activities.insight: Parallel lines never meet and stay the same distance apart; segments or sides are parallel when they lie on such lines, whatever their lengths; perpendicular means a square corner at any orientation, so rotating a figure does not change whether an angle is a right angle.

activities.title: Mark the tilted trapezoid
steps: On a right trapezoid (a trapezoid with right angles) drawn deliberately tilted off-axis, mark a right angle (90°), an acute angle (<90°) and an obtuse angle (between 90° and 180°).
Identify and mark every pair of parallel sides, including pairs where the two sides have different lengths.
Draw a ray and a line segment side by side and explain the difference (a ray extends without end in one direction; a segment stops at both endpoints; a line extends without end both ways).
Justify each mark by its defining property — square corner, never-meeting/equidistant, opening — rather than by how upright or how long the lines look.
activities.insight: The defining property, not the orientation or drawn length, decides whether an element is a right/acute/obtuse angle, parallel, or perpendicular; rays, segments and lines differ by where (or whether) they stop.

activities.title: Vocabulary reference and identification check-up
steps: Use a labelled figure — ray vs segment vs line, right/acute/obtuse angles, a parallel pair and a perpendicular pair — as a glossary, naming each element and its defining property.
Sort a set of angles in tilted figures into right, acute and obtuse, including a comparison pair of EQUAL angles drawn with clearly unequal arm lengths (which should be judged equal).
Separately, pick out all pairs of parallel sides in a trapezoid, including a pair whose two sides have different lengths.
After the hands-on work, re-state in your own words why arm length and orientation do not change an element's category.
activities.insight: Correct vocabulary and identification should rest on defining properties that transfer to tilted and unequal-length figures, not on upright prototypes.

checkQuestion: Put a ruler and a printed figure in front of the child — a trapezoid drawn tilted off-axis, with two extra straight lines crossing nearby — plus a blank space. Say: 'Draw me one pair of parallel lines and one pair of perpendicular lines. Then on this shape, mark a right angle, an acute angle and an obtuse angle, and show me every pair of parallel sides.' Watch how they draw and mark — do not ask them to define the words.
checkAnswer: Draws two never-meeting, equidistant lines (any orientation) as parallel and two lines meeting at a square corner as perpendicular; on the tilted trapezoid marks a 90° angle as right, a <90° as acute and a >90° as obtuse, and identifies the pair(s) of parallel sides — judging by defining property (square corner / never-meeting / opening), orientation- and length-independent, not by how 'upright' or how long the lines look.
